definition: Transformative means causing a major, lasting change.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word transformative. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know transformative should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: One librarian's summer reading list proved transformative, turning a bored ten-year-old into the historian she is today.
An eye-opening trip shows you what you hadn't seen; a transformative one goes further — you come home someone slightly different.
Revolutionary outruns even transformative: the transformative reform remakes the school, while the revolutionary one sweeps the old school away and starts over.

Life-changing is the everyday phrase for an experience that redirects the course of one person's life — a diagnosis, a scholarship, a chance meeting — though overuse has worn it soft. Transformative is broader and more formal: policies, technologies, and working habits can all be transformative, remaking whatever they touch, not only a life.

Groundbreaking praises novelty: the first of its kind, breaking ground where nothing stood before. It says nothing about what happens to anyone afterward. Transformative measures the aftermath instead — a major change that lasts — and something quite ordinary, an old drill or a strict teacher, can still be transformative.

Veterans call the silence transformative — forced to listen, they finally hear which jokes land and which chapters die, and they say they never wrote, or read, the same way again.
The rule doesn't just improve their drafts; it rewires the drafter.
Transformative claims more than helpful or eye-opening: it says the change is major, and it keeps — the thing changed is now a different thing.
An eye-opening lecture shows you a new view; a transformative one leaves you someone who can't unsee it.
If everything snaps back by Friday, the word was too big.
Save transformative for changes that are both major and lasting — the experience or policy after which the thing is different in kind.
It describes the cause of change; this unit's dynamic describes a state of ongoing change.
A dynamic decade contains a thousand changes; a transformative one leaves a changed world.

The steel box that remade world trade was not an invention so much as a decision.
Crates, trucks, and cranes all existed in 1956; Malcom McLean's contribution was a standard size, agreed on by everyone.

Economists rank that plain box among the most transformative objects of the century: within twenty years it had redrawn ports, shrunk crews, rerouted whole industries, and dropped the cost of moving goods to a rounding error.
Purists note that nothing in it was technically novel.
That is close to the point.
The measure of the box was never its cleverness.
It was how much of the world looked different once the box had passed through it — and stayed different.
